---
title: "Kernels that output functions: matrix- and operator-valued kernels"
description: "From one output to many to a whole function. Matrix-valued kernels, coregionalisation, the Kronecker trick, operator-valued kernels and their RKHS, and Gaussian processes that learn operators. Every step derived."
date: 2024-06-27
updated: 2026-10-26
cover: /blog/thumbs/operator.png
tags: [kernels, operator-learning, gaussian-processes, tutorial]
---

Many questions in science map a function to a function. An initial temperature profile determines the profile an hour later; a permeability field determines a pressure field; today's atmosphere determines tomorrow's. Such a map is an **operator** $\mathcal{G} : \mathcal{U} \to \mathcal{V}$ between spaces of functions, and learning it from examples is *operator learning*.

Below, a model has seen 40 pairs (input profile, profile after heat diffusion). Draw any input in the top panel. The bottom panel shows the true output (dashed) and the model's prediction with a $\pm 2$ standard-deviation band. Try **Add a wiggle** or **Double it**, and switch the kernel.

<figure class="fig" data-operator>
  <canvas data-figure="operator" style="height:380px" aria-label="Draw an input function; the learned heat operator predicts the output with an uncertainty band."></canvas>
  <div class="controls">
    <div class="seg" role="group" aria-label="Input kernel">
      <button type="button" data-k="linear" class="on">Linear kernel</button>
      <button type="button" data-k="rbf">RBF kernel</button>
    </div>
    <button type="button" data-new>New input</button>
    <button type="button" data-wiggle>Add a wiggle</button>
    <button type="button" data-double>Double it</button>
  </div>
  <figcaption><span class="mono" data-out></span></figcaption>
</figure>

Three things are worth noticing, and the rest of the post explains each:

1. For inputs like the training data, the prediction is almost exact and the band is almost zero.
2. **Add a wiggle** injects a frequency no training input contained. The band widens: the model reports that it has not seen this, which is exactly the "knows what it doesn't know" property of the [GP post](/aboutme/blog/understanding-gaussian-processes/), now for function-valued outputs.
3. **Double it** with the linear kernel still predicts well, because heat diffusion is linear. With the RBF kernel, the prediction falls apart and the band widens to cover the error: an RBF kernel only trusts inputs near the ones it has seen. The kernel on *inputs* is an assumption about the operator.

The route has three steps, one output at a time: a scalar output (Section 1), a vector of outputs (Section 2), a whole function of outputs (Sections 3 to 5). It assumes the [GP post](/aboutme/blog/understanding-gaussian-processes/), whose lemmas are cited as "GP Lemma 5" and so on. Proofs, notes, remarks and examples are folded; open them as needed.

The figure fixes the shapes. Everything in Sections 2 to 5 is about the right-hand column: what the blocks mean, when the big matrix is a valid covariance, and which assumptions make it small enough to use.


## Notation

Plain italic letters are scalars or elements of a function space ($u$, $v$, $\alpha_i$). Bold italic lower-case letters are vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ ($\boldsymbol{x}$, $\boldsymbol{c}$). Bold upright capitals are matrices ($\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{B}$). Calligraphic letters are operators or spaces.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\mathcal{X}$, $\boldsymbol{x}_i$ | input space, training inputs (Sections 1–2) |
| $\mathcal{U}$, $\mathcal{V}$ | input and output function spaces; $\mathcal{V}$ a separable Hilbert space, e.g. $L^2(\Omega)$ |
| $u_i \in \mathcal{U}$, $v_i \in \mathcal{V}$ | training input and output functions |
| $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{V}}$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathcal{V}}$ | inner product and norm of $\mathcal{V}$ |
| $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{V})$ | bounded linear operators on $\mathcal{V}$; $\mathcal{A}^*$ is the adjoint |
| $k$, $\mathbf{K}$ | scalar kernel, its $N\times N$ Gram matrix |
| $\boldsymbol{K}(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}') \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ | matrix-valued kernel (Section 2) |
| $\mathcal{K}(u, u') \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{V})$ | operator-valued kernel; never the Gram matrix $\mathbf{K}$ |
| $\mathbb{K}$ | block Gram matrix or operator, blocks $\boldsymbol{K}(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}_j)$ or $\mathcal{K}(u_i, u_j)$ |
| $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathcal{T}$ | output covariance in a separable kernel: a matrix, an operator |
| $\mathcal{H}_k$, $\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}$ | RKHS of a scalar, of an operator-valued kernel |
| $\otimes$ | Kronecker product |
| $\lambda$ | regularisation (equivalently noise) parameter |

## 1. One output: the RKHS in one page

Recall from GP Definition 2 that a kernel $k$ is positive definite when every Gram matrix is positive semidefinite. Each kernel comes with a space of functions it can represent.

:::definition[Reproducing kernel Hilbert space]
The RKHS $\mathcal{H}_k$ of a positive-definite kernel $k$ on $\mathcal{X}$ is the completion of the set of finite combinations $f = \sum_j a_j\,k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}_j)$ under the inner product

$$
\Big\langle \sum_i a_i\,k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}_i),\; \sum_j b_j\,k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}'_j) \Big\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_k} = \sum_{i,j} a_i\,b_j\,k(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}'_j).
$$
:::

:::lemma[Reproducing property]
For every $f \in \mathcal{H}_k$ and $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{X}$, $\;f(\boldsymbol{x}) = \langle f, k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_k}$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Finite combinations.** Take $f = \sum_j a_j\,k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}_j)$ and note that $k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x})$ is the combination with one coefficient, $1$, at the point $\boldsymbol{x}$.

**Step 2. Apply the definition of the inner product.**

$$
\langle f, k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_k} = \sum_j a_j \cdot 1 \cdot k(\boldsymbol{x}_j, \boldsymbol{x}) = \sum_j a_j\,k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_j) = f(\boldsymbol{x}),
$$

using the symmetry $k(\boldsymbol{x}_j, \boldsymbol{x}) = k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_j)$.

**Step 3. Limits.** Both sides are continuous in $f$ (the right side by Cauchy–Schwarz), so the identity passes from finite combinations to their limits.
:::

:::remark[What the RKHS norm measures]
**Step 1.** By the reproducing property and linearity, $f(\boldsymbol{x}) - f(\boldsymbol{x}') = \langle f,\, k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}) - k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}')\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_k}$.

**Step 2.** Cauchy–Schwarz gives

$$
\lvert f(\boldsymbol{x}) - f(\boldsymbol{x}')\rvert \le \lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_k}\; \lVert k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}) - k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}')\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_k}.
$$

**Step 3.** Expanding the last norm with the inner product, $\lVert k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}) - k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}')\rVert^2 = k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}) - 2k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}') + k(\boldsymbol{x}', \boldsymbol{x}')$, which is small when the kernel regards $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}'$ as similar.

So a function with a small RKHS norm cannot change much between points the kernel considers close. Penalising $\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_k}$ penalises roughness *as the kernel defines it*.
:::

:::theorem[Representer theorem, kernel ridge regression]
Given data $\{(\boldsymbol{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ and $\lambda > 0$, the minimiser of

$$
J(f) = \sum_{i=1}^N \big(y_i - f(\boldsymbol{x}_i)\big)^2 + \lambda\,\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_k}^2
$$

over $\mathcal{H}_k$ is $\hat f(\boldsymbol{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i\,k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_i)$ with $\boldsymbol{\alpha} = (\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{y}$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Split $f$.** Let $\mathcal{S} = \operatorname{span}\{k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}_i)\}_{i=1}^N$, a finite-dimensional (hence closed) subspace. Every $f$ decomposes uniquely as $f = f_{\mathcal{S}} + f_\perp$ with $f_{\mathcal{S}} \in \mathcal{S}$ and $f_\perp \perp \mathcal{S}$.

**Step 2. The orthogonal part is invisible at the data.** By the reproducing property, $f_\perp(\boldsymbol{x}_i) = \langle f_\perp, k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}_i)\rangle = 0$, so $f(\boldsymbol{x}_i) = f_{\mathcal{S}}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$ for every $i$.

**Step 3. The orthogonal part only adds norm.** By Pythagoras, $\lVert f\rVert^2 = \lVert f_{\mathcal{S}}\rVert^2 + \lVert f_\perp\rVert^2$.

**Step 4. Conclude that $f_\perp = 0$.** By Steps 2 and 3, $J(f) = J(f_{\mathcal{S}}) + \lambda\lVert f_\perp\rVert^2 \ge J(f_{\mathcal{S}})$, with equality only if $f_\perp = 0$. So the minimiser lies in $\mathcal{S}$: $\hat f = \sum_i \alpha_i\,k(\cdot, \boldsymbol{x}_i)$.

**Step 5. Write $J$ in terms of $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$.** The fitted values are $\hat f(\boldsymbol{x}_i) = (\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\alpha})_i$, and the definition of the inner product gives $\lVert\hat f\rVert^2 = \boldsymbol{\alpha}^\top\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\alpha}$. So

$$
J(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) = (\boldsymbol{y} - \mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\alpha})^\top(\boldsymbol{y} - \mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\alpha}) + \lambda\,\boldsymbol{\alpha}^\top\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\alpha}.
$$

**Step 6. Set the gradient to zero.** Using $\mathbf{K}^\top = \mathbf{K}$,

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}J = -2\mathbf{K}(\boldsymbol{y} - \mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\alpha}) + 2\lambda\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\alpha} = 2\mathbf{K}\big((\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\boldsymbol{\alpha} - \boldsymbol{y}\big) = \mathbf{0}.
$$

**Step 7. Solve.** $\boldsymbol{\alpha} = (\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{y}$ satisfies Step 6. ($\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I}$ is positive definite, hence invertible. If $\mathbf{K}$ is singular other $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ also satisfy Step 6, but they give the same function $\hat f$.)
:::

The kernel ridge regression predictor $\hat f(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{k}(\boldsymbol{x})^\top(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{y}$ is exactly the GP posterior mean with noise variance $\sigma_n^2 = \lambda$ (GP Proposition 4). The GP adds what kernel ridge regression lacks: a variance.

## 2. Many outputs: matrix-valued kernels

Now each input has $p$ outputs: the temperature *and* humidity at a station, the angles of every joint in a robot arm. Fitting $p$ separate models throws away what one output says about another. A matrix-valued kernel keeps it.

:::definition[Matrix-valued kernel]
A function $\boldsymbol{K} : \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ is a positive-definite matrix-valued kernel if $\boldsymbol{K}(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')^\top = \boldsymbol{K}(\boldsymbol{x}', \boldsymbol{x})$ and, for all finite sets $\{\boldsymbol{x}_i\}_{i=1}^N$ and vectors $\{\boldsymbol{c}_i\}_{i=1}^N \subset \mathbb{R}^p$,

$$
\sum_{i,j=1}^N \boldsymbol{c}_i^\top\,\boldsymbol{K}(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}_j)\,\boldsymbol{c}_j \ge 0 .
$$

Equivalently, the $Np\times Np$ block Gram matrix $\mathbb{K}$ with blocks $\boldsymbol{K}(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}_j)$ is positive semidefinite.
:::

In GP terms, $\boldsymbol{f} \sim \mathcal{GP}(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{K})$ is a random function with values in $\mathbb{R}^p$ and $\operatorname{Cov}[\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}), \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}')] = \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}')^\top] = \boldsymbol{K}(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')$. Entry $(a, b)$ is the covariance between output $a$ at $\boldsymbol{x}$ and output $b$ at $\boldsymbol{x}'$. The transpose condition holds because $\operatorname{Cov}[\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}), \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}')]^\top = \operatorname{Cov}[\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}'), \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})]$.

### Separable kernels and the Kronecker product

The simplest useful choice multiplies a scalar kernel by a fixed matrix: $\boldsymbol{K}(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}') = k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')\,\mathbf{B}$. The scalar kernel says how inputs relate; $\mathbf{B}$ says how outputs relate. Its block Gram matrix is a Kronecker product.

:::definition[Kronecker product]
For $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and $\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$, $\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}$ is the $np\times np$ block matrix whose $(i, j)$ block is $a_{ij}\mathbf{B}$.
:::

So with the data stacked input by input, the block Gram matrix of $k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')\mathbf{B}$ is $\mathbb{K} = \mathbf{K} \otimes \mathbf{B}$.

:::lemma[Mixed product and its consequences]
For conformable matrices,

1. $(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B})(\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{D}) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C}) \otimes (\mathbf{B}\mathbf{D})$;
2. $(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B})^{-1} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{B}^{-1}$ when both are invertible;
3. if $\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{u} = \lambda\boldsymbol{u}$ and $\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{v} = \kappa\boldsymbol{v}$, then $(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B})(\boldsymbol{u} \otimes \boldsymbol{v}) = \lambda\kappa\,(\boldsymbol{u} \otimes \boldsymbol{v})$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Multiply block by block.** Block $(i, j)$ of the product is the sum over $l$ of block $(i, l)$ of the first factor times block $(l, j)$ of the second:

$$
\sum_l (a_{il}\mathbf{B})(c_{lj}\mathbf{D}) = \Big(\sum_l a_{il}c_{lj}\Big)\mathbf{B}\mathbf{D} = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C})_{ij}\,\mathbf{B}\mathbf{D},
$$

which is block $(i, j)$ of $(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C}) \otimes (\mathbf{B}\mathbf{D})$. This is part 1.

**Step 2. Inverse.** By part 1, $(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B})(\mathbf{A}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{B}^{-1}) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1}) \otimes (\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^{-1}) = \mathbf{I} \otimes \mathbf{I} = \mathbf{I}$. This is part 2.

**Step 3. Eigenvectors.** A vector is a one-column matrix, so part 1 applies: $(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B})(\boldsymbol{u} \otimes \boldsymbol{v}) = (\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{u}) \otimes (\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{v}) = (\lambda\boldsymbol{u}) \otimes (\kappa\boldsymbol{v}) = \lambda\kappa\,(\boldsymbol{u} \otimes \boldsymbol{v})$. This is part 3.
:::

:::proposition[Separable kernels are valid]
If $k$ is a positive-definite scalar kernel and $\mathbf{B}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, then $k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')\mathbf{B}$ is a positive-definite matrix-valued kernel.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Symmetry.** $\big(k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')\mathbf{B}\big)^\top = k(\boldsymbol{x}', \boldsymbol{x})\,\mathbf{B}^\top = k(\boldsymbol{x}', \boldsymbol{x})\,\mathbf{B}$.

**Step 2. Eigendecompose both factors.** $\mathbf{K} = \sum_i \lambda_i\boldsymbol{u}_i\boldsymbol{u}_i^\top$ and $\mathbf{B} = \sum_j \kappa_j\boldsymbol{v}_j\boldsymbol{v}_j^\top$, with orthonormal eigenvectors and $\lambda_i, \kappa_j \ge 0$.

**Step 3. Eigenvectors of the block Gram matrix.** By Lemma 2, part 3, each $\boldsymbol{u}_i \otimes \boldsymbol{v}_j$ is an eigenvector of $\mathbf{K} \otimes \mathbf{B}$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_i\kappa_j \ge 0$.

**Step 4. They are all of them.** The $Np$ vectors $\boldsymbol{u}_i \otimes \boldsymbol{v}_j$ are orthonormal, since by part 1, $(\boldsymbol{u}_i \otimes \boldsymbol{v}_j)^\top(\boldsymbol{u}_{i'} \otimes \boldsymbol{v}_{j'}) = (\boldsymbol{u}_i^\top\boldsymbol{u}_{i'})(\boldsymbol{v}_j^\top\boldsymbol{v}_{j'})$, which is $1$ if $(i, j) = (i', j')$ and $0$ otherwise. So they form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^{Np}$.

**Step 5. Conclude.** A symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues are all non-negative is positive semidefinite.
:::

:::example[What B means, in three cases]
- $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{I}$: the outputs are independent GPs that share a kernel. Nothing is borrowed.
- $\mathbf{B} = \boldsymbol{1}\boldsymbol{1}^\top$ (all entries $1$): every output is the same function.
- $\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: write $f_2 = \rho f_1 + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\,g$ with $f_1, g$ independent GPs with kernel $k$. Then

  **Step 1.** $\operatorname{Cov}[f_2(\boldsymbol{x}), f_1(\boldsymbol{x}')] = \rho\,k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')$, because $g$ is independent of $f_1$.

  **Step 2.** $\operatorname{Cov}[f_2(\boldsymbol{x}), f_2(\boldsymbol{x}')] = \rho^2k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}') + (1 - \rho^2)\,k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}') = k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')$.

  So $\rho$ is literally the share of output 2 that is output 1. This is the *intrinsic coregionalisation model*; summing several such terms, $\sum_q k_q(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')\mathbf{B}_q$, gives the *linear model of coregionalisation* from geostatistics.
:::

Output 2 below is observed only on the left. Move $\rho$ and watch its posterior on the shaded part, where it has no data of its own. The block Gram matrix on the right shows the off-diagonal blocks, $\rho\,k(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}_j)$, that carry the information across.

<figure class="fig" data-coreg>
  <canvas data-figure="coreg" style="height:360px" aria-label="Two correlated outputs; output 2 borrows strength from output 1 as the correlation grows."></canvas>
  <figcaption><label class="slider">correlation ρ <input type="range" min="-0.95" max="0.95" step="0.01" value="0.9" data-rho /></label> <span class="mono" data-out></span></figcaption>
</figure>

At $\rho \approx 0.9$, output 2 on the right follows the shape of output 1's data, and its band shrinks well below the prior. At $\rho = 0$ it falls back to the prior there. At $\rho \approx -0.9$ it follows the *mirror image* of output 1. The truth has $\rho \approx 0.9$, so only that setting is right; learning $\mathbf{B}$ from data (by the marginal likelihood, GP Section 7) is how the model finds out.

### Fitting all outputs at once: the Kronecker trick

The representer theorem carries over (proved in full in Section 4, Theorem 2 with $\mathcal{V} = \mathbb{R}^p$): the fit is $\hat{\boldsymbol{f}}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \sum_i \boldsymbol{K}(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_i)\,\boldsymbol{c}_i$ with $(\mathbb{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\boldsymbol{c} = \boldsymbol{y}$, where $\boldsymbol{c}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}$ stack the $\boldsymbol{c}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{y}_i$. Solved directly this costs $O(N^3p^3)$. For a separable kernel with every output observed at every input, it costs far less.

:::proposition[The Kronecker trick]
Let $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times p}$ have rows $\boldsymbol{y}_i^\top$, and let $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top$ and $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^\top$ be eigendecompositions, with $\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)$ and $\mathbf{D} = \operatorname{diag}(\kappa_j)$. The coefficient matrix $\mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times p}$ (rows $\boldsymbol{c}_i^\top$) is

$$
\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{U}\,\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\,\mathbf{V}^\top,
\qquad
\tilde C_{ij} = \frac{(\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{V})_{ij}}{\lambda_i\kappa_j + \lambda},
$$

at cost $O(N^3 + p^3 + N^2p + Np^2)$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Predictions in matrix form.** Row $i$ of the fitted values is $\hat{\boldsymbol{f}}(\boldsymbol{x}_i)^\top = \sum_j k(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}_j)\,\boldsymbol{c}_j^\top\mathbf{B}$ (transpose of $\sum_j k\,\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{c}_j$, with $\mathbf{B}^\top = \mathbf{B}$). Stacking the rows, the matrix of fitted values is $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{B}$.

**Step 2. The linear system in matrix form.** Row $i$ of $(\mathbb{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})\boldsymbol{c} = \boldsymbol{y}$ reads $\sum_j k(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}_j)\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{c}_j + \lambda\boldsymbol{c}_i = \boldsymbol{y}_i$. Transposing each and stacking, by Step 1:

$$
\mathbf{K}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{B} + \lambda\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{Y}.
$$

**Step 3. Rotate into both eigenbases.** Substitute $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top$ and $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^\top$, multiply on the left by $\mathbf{U}^\top$ and on the right by $\mathbf{V}$, and use $\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{V}^\top\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}$. With $\tilde{\mathbf{C}} = \mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{C}\mathbf{V}$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{V}$:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\mathbf{D} + \lambda\tilde{\mathbf{C}} = \tilde{\mathbf{Y}}.
$$

**Step 4. The system is now diagonal.** Because $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are diagonal, entry $(i, j)$ of $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\mathbf{D}$ is $\lambda_i\tilde C_{ij}\kappa_j$. So every entry is its own scalar equation, $(\lambda_i\kappa_j + \lambda)\tilde C_{ij} = \tilde Y_{ij}$.

**Step 5. Solve and rotate back.** Divide entrywise, then $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{U}\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\mathbf{V}^\top$ (invert Step 3's rotation).

**Step 6. Cost.** Two eigendecompositions, $O(N^3)$ and $O(p^3)$; the products $\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{U}\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\mathbf{V}^\top$ cost $O(N^2p + Np^2)$.
:::

The saving is dramatic exactly when outputs are functions. On a grid of $p = 4096$ points with $N = 1000$ training pairs, the direct system has four million unknowns; the Kronecker route needs two moderate eigendecompositions.

```python
import numpy as np

def fit_separable(K, B, Y, lam):
    """Solve K C B + lam C = Y for C (N x p) with two eigendecompositions."""
    lk, U = np.linalg.eigh(K)                    # K = U diag(lk) U^T
    lb, V = np.linalg.eigh(B)                    # B = V diag(lb) V^T
    Ct = (U.T @ Y @ V) / (np.outer(lk, lb) + lam)
    return U @ Ct @ V.T

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, p, lam = 30, 4, 1e-2
X = rng.uniform(size=(N, 1))
K = np.exp(-0.5 * (X - X.T) ** 2 / 0.2**2)       # scalar RBF Gram matrix
A = rng.standard_normal((p, p)); B = A @ A.T / p   # any positive semidefinite B
Y = rng.standard_normal((N, p))

# Check against the direct (N p) x (N p) solve, with blocks k(x_i, x_j) B
big = np.kron(K, B) + lam * np.eye(N * p)
assert np.allclose(fit_separable(K, B, Y, lam).reshape(-1), np.linalg.solve(big, Y.reshape(-1)))
```

## 3. Function outputs: operator-valued kernels

Now each output is a function $v \in \mathcal{V}$, say $\mathcal{V} = L^2(\Omega)$. Replace "a $p\times p$ matrix" by "a bounded linear operator on $\mathcal{V}$", and "$\boldsymbol{c}^\top\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{c}'$" by "$\langle c, \mathcal{A}c'\rangle_{\mathcal{V}}$". Nothing else changes.

:::definition[Operator-valued kernel]
A map $\mathcal{K} : \mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{U} \to \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{V})$ is a positive-definite operator-valued kernel if $\mathcal{K}(u, u')^* = \mathcal{K}(u', u)$ and, for all finite sets $\{u_i\}_{i=1}^N \subset \mathcal{U}$ and $\{c_i\}_{i=1}^N \subset \mathcal{V}$,

$$
\sum_{i,j=1}^N \big\langle c_i,\; \mathcal{K}(u_i, u_j)\,c_j\big\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} \ge 0 .
$$

With $\mathcal{V} = \mathbb{R}^p$ this is Definition 2.
:::

The scalar kernel $k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}') = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\boldsymbol{x})^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_w\boldsymbol{\phi}(\boldsymbol{x}')$ came from features (GP Proposition 3). Operator-valued kernels come from *feature operators* the same way.

:::proposition[Kernels from feature operators]
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a Hilbert space and, for each $u$, let $\Phi(u) : \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{V}$ be a bounded linear operator. Then $\mathcal{K}(u, u') = \Phi(u)\,\Phi(u')^*$ is a positive-definite operator-valued kernel.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Symmetry.** The adjoint reverses products and $(\mathcal{A}^*)^* = \mathcal{A}$, so $\big(\Phi(u)\Phi(u')^*\big)^* = \Phi(u')\Phi(u)^*$, which is $\mathcal{K}(u', u)$.

**Step 2. Move each operator across the inner product** using the definition of the adjoint, $\langle c, \Phi(u)g\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} = \langle\Phi(u)^*c, g\rangle_{\mathcal{F}}$:

$$
\big\langle c_i,\, \Phi(u_i)\Phi(u_j)^*c_j\big\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} = \big\langle\Phi(u_i)^*c_i,\; \Phi(u_j)^*c_j\big\rangle_{\mathcal{F}}.
$$

**Step 3. Recognise a squared norm.** Summing over $i$ and $j$ and using bilinearity,

$$
\sum_{i,j}\big\langle c_i,\, \mathcal{K}(u_i, u_j)c_j\big\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} = \Big\lVert\sum_i\Phi(u_i)^*c_i\Big\rVert_{\mathcal{F}}^2 \ge 0 .
$$
:::

:::definition[Vector-valued RKHS]
The RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}$ is the completion of finite combinations $f = \sum_j \mathcal{K}(\cdot, u_j)\,c_j$ (functions from $\mathcal{U}$ to $\mathcal{V}$) under

$$
\big\langle\mathcal{K}(\cdot, u)\,c,\; \mathcal{K}(\cdot, u')\,c'\big\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}} = \big\langle c,\; \mathcal{K}(u, u')\,c'\big\rangle_{\mathcal{V}},
$$

extended bilinearly (Micchelli and Pontil, 2005; Carmeli, De Vito and Toigo, 2006).
:::

:::lemma[Reproducing property, vector-valued]
For all $f \in \mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}$, $u \in \mathcal{U}$ and $c \in \mathcal{V}$: $\;\langle f(u), c\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} = \langle f,\, \mathcal{K}(\cdot, u)\,c\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}}$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Finite combinations.** Take $f = \sum_j \mathcal{K}(\cdot, u_j)\,c_j$. By the definition of the inner product,

$$
\langle f, \mathcal{K}(\cdot, u)\,c\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}} = \sum_j \big\langle c_j,\, \mathcal{K}(u_j, u)\,c\big\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} .
$$

**Step 2. Move the operator across.** By the adjoint and the symmetry of Definition 4, $\langle c_j, \mathcal{K}(u_j, u)c\rangle = \langle\mathcal{K}(u_j, u)^*c_j, c\rangle = \langle\mathcal{K}(u, u_j)c_j, c\rangle$.

**Step 3. Sum.** $\sum_j\langle\mathcal{K}(u, u_j)c_j, c\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} = \langle f(u), c\rangle_{\mathcal{V}}$. Limits pass as in Lemma 1.
:::

### Currying: an operator-valued kernel is a scalar kernel on pairs

Operator-valued kernels look exotic. One change of viewpoint makes them ordinary. A map $f : \mathcal{U} \to \mathcal{V}$ that sends an input $u$ to an output *function* $f(u)$ carries exactly the same information as a scalar function of two arguments, $g(u, z) = f(u)(z)$, where $z \in \Omega$ is a location in the output domain. Passing from $g$ to $f$ is called *currying* in functional programming.

trick</text></svg></figure>

:::proposition[Currying turns scalar kernels on pairs into operator-valued kernels]
Let $\mathcal{V} = L^2(\Omega)$ and let $\kappa$ be a bounded, continuous, positive-definite scalar kernel on pairs $(u, z) \in \mathcal{U}\times\Omega$. Define

$$
\big(\mathcal{K}(u, u')\,c\big)(z) = \int_\Omega\kappa\big((u, z), (u', z')\big)\,c(z')\,dz' .
$$

Then $\mathcal{K}$ is a positive-definite operator-valued kernel. Moreover, if $g \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, \kappa)$ on $\mathcal{U}\times\Omega$ and $f(u) = g(u, \cdot)$, then $\mathbb{E}\big[\langle f(u), a\rangle\langle f(u'), b\rangle\big] = \langle a, \mathcal{K}(u, u')\,b\rangle$: the curried GP is a $\mathcal{V}$-valued GP with kernel $\mathcal{K}$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Symmetry.** The adjoint of an integral operator swaps the two arguments of its kernel. Since $\kappa\big((u, z), (u', z')\big) = \kappa\big((u', z'), (u, z)\big)$, the adjoint of $\mathcal{K}(u, u')$ is $\mathcal{K}(u', u)$.

**Step 2. Write the quadratic form as a double integral.** By the definition of the $L^2$ inner product,

$$
\sum_{i,j}\big\langle c_i, \mathcal{K}(u_i, u_j)\,c_j\big\rangle = \int_\Omega\int_\Omega\sum_{i,j}c_i(z)\,\kappa\big((u_i, z), (u_j, z')\big)\,c_j(z')\,dz\,dz' .
$$

**Step 3. It is a limit of non-negative numbers.** Replace both integrals by Riemann sums over points $z_1, \dots, z_m$ with cell size $\Delta$. The result is $\sum_{(i,p),(j,q)}\gamma_{ip}\,\kappa\big((u_i, z_p), (u_j, z_q)\big)\,\gamma_{jq}$ with $\gamma_{ip} = c_i(z_p)\Delta$: a quadratic form of $\kappa$ on the finite set of pairs $\{(u_i, z_p)\}$, hence $\ge 0$. As $\Delta \to 0$ the sums converge to the integral (for continuous $c_i$, then by density for all of $L^2$), and a limit of non-negative numbers is non-negative.

**Step 4. The covariance of the curried GP.** $\langle f(u), a\rangle = \int_\Omega g(u, z)\,a(z)\,dz$. Multiply two such integrals and exchange expectation and integration (Fubini, using boundedness of $\kappa$):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\big[\langle f(u), a\rangle\langle f(u'), b\rangle\big]
&= \iint a(z)\,\mathbb{E}\big[g(u, z)\,g(u', z')\big]\,b(z')\,dz\,dz' \\
&= \iint a(z)\,\kappa\big((u, z), (u', z')\big)\,b(z')\,dz\,dz' = \langle a, \mathcal{K}(u, u')\,b\rangle .
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5. Gaussianity.** Each $\langle f(u), a\rangle$ is a limit of finite linear combinations of the jointly Gaussian values $g(u, z_p)$, so any finite collection of them is jointly Gaussian (GP Lemma 2, then limits).
:::

Three things become obvious in the scalar view.

- **Separable means product.** $\mathcal{K}(u, u') = k(u, u')\,\mathcal{T}$, with $\mathcal{T}$ the integral operator of $t(z, z')$, is the curried form of the product kernel $\kappa\big((u, z), (u', z')\big) = k(u, u')\,t(z, z')$. On $N$ inputs and a shared grid of $m$ points, entry $\big((i, p), (j, q)\big)$ of the Gram matrix is $k(u_i, u_j)\,t(z_p, z_q)$, which is entry $\big((i, p), (j, q)\big)$ of $\mathbf{K} \otimes \mathbf{T}$. The Kronecker trick of Section 2 is the classical trick for product kernels on grids.
- **Outputs need not share a grid.** In the scalar view an output observed at its own scattered locations is just more scalar data at pairs $(u_i, z)$. The model is unchanged; only the Kronecker structure, and its speed, is lost.
- **Resolution-agnostic prediction comes for free.** The posterior is a GP on pairs, so it can be queried at any $z$, on any grid, after training.

:::remark[Linearised neural operators are curried GPs]
Magnani, Pförtner, Weber and Hennig (ICML 2025) use this view to give a trained neural operator $\mathcal{G}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ an uncertainty, in four steps.

**Step 1. A Gaussian belief over weights.** For example a Laplace approximation around the trained weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}_*$: $\boldsymbol{\theta} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_*, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\theta})$, with $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\theta}$ the inverse Hessian of the training loss.

**Step 2. Linearise in the weights.** $\mathcal{G}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(u)(z) \approx \mathcal{G}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_*}(u)(z) + \boldsymbol{j}(u, z)^\top(\boldsymbol{\theta} - \boldsymbol{\theta}_*)$, with $\boldsymbol{j}(u, z) = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{G}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(u)(z)$ at $\boldsymbol{\theta}_*$.

**Step 3. An affine map of a Gaussian is Gaussian** (GP Lemma 2). For every finite set of pairs $(u, z)$ the outputs are jointly Gaussian, so $g(u, z) = \mathcal{G}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(u)(z)$ is a scalar GP with mean $\mathcal{G}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_*}(u)(z)$ and kernel $\kappa\big((u, z), (u', z')\big) = \boldsymbol{j}(u, z)^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\theta}\,\boldsymbol{j}(u', z')$.

**Step 4. Curry.** By Proposition 4 this is a function-valued GP over output functions. They call it probabilistic currying; it is resolution-agnostic and needs no retraining.

The kernel in Step 3 is the weight-space kernel of GP Proposition 3, with the network's Jacobian as the feature map.
:::

### Separable operator kernels, and why the output covariance must be trace class

The workhorse is again separable: $\mathcal{K}(u, u') = k(u, u')\,\mathcal{T}$, where $k$ is a scalar kernel on input functions and $\mathcal{T}$ is a self-adjoint positive semidefinite operator on $\mathcal{V}$. In the GP view, $f(u)$ is a random function with covariance operator $k(u, u)\,\mathcal{T}$: **$\mathcal{T}$ decides what the predicted outputs look like.** A natural choice is an integral operator, $(\mathcal{T}c)(z) = \int_\Omega t(z, z')\,c(z')\,dz'$, with a Matérn or RBF kernel $t$ on the output domain. A tempting choice, $\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{I}$, fails, and the reason is worth a proposition.

:::proposition[Expected squared norm of a Gaussian random function]
Let $f$ be a centred Gaussian random element of $\mathcal{V}$ with covariance operator $\mathcal{C}$, meaning $\mathbb{E}\big[\langle f, a\rangle\langle f, b\rangle\big] = \langle a, \mathcal{C}b\rangle$ for all $a, b \in \mathcal{V}$. Then $\mathbb{E}\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{V}}^2 = \operatorname{tr}\mathcal{C}$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Expand in a basis.** For an orthonormal basis $\{e_n\}$ of $\mathcal{V}$, Parseval's identity gives $\lVert f\rVert^2 = \sum_n\langle f, e_n\rangle^2$.

**Step 2. Take expectations term by term.** Every term is non-negative, so the expectation of the sum is the sum of the expectations (monotone convergence):

$$
\mathbb{E}\lVert f\rVert^2 = \sum_n\mathbb{E}\big[\langle f, e_n\rangle^2\big].
$$

**Step 3. Use the definition of $\mathcal{C}$** with $a = b = e_n$: $\mathbb{E}[\langle f, e_n\rangle^2] = \langle e_n, \mathcal{C}e_n\rangle$.

**Step 4. Recognise the trace.** $\sum_n\langle e_n, \mathcal{C}e_n\rangle = \operatorname{tr}\mathcal{C}$, by definition of the trace.
:::

So predicted outputs have finite energy only if $\operatorname{tr}\big(k(u, u)\,\mathcal{T}\big) < \infty$, that is, only if $\mathcal{T}$ is **trace class**. The identity has $\operatorname{tr}\mathcal{I} = \sum_n 1 = \infty$: a "GP with covariance $\mathcal{I}$" is white noise, not a function. For an integral operator with continuous kernel on a compact domain, $\operatorname{tr}\mathcal{T} = \int_\Omega t(z, z)\,dz < \infty$ (Mercer's theorem), so smooth output covariances are safe.

:::note[How this shows up in code]
On a grid of $m$ points, $\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{I}$ becomes $\mathbf{I}_m$, whose trace is $m$. Every sample's squared norm grows linearly with the resolution, and refining the mesh changes the model. A trace-class $\mathcal{T}$, discretised with quadrature weights, has a trace that converges as $m$ grows. "Resolution-independent" is a statement about traces.
:::

## 4. Kernel regression for operators

Given pairs $\{(u_i, v_i)\}_{i=1}^N$, minimise $\sum_i\lVert v_i - f(u_i)\rVert_{\mathcal{V}}^2 + \lambda\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}}^2$ over $f \in \mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}$. The splitting proof of Theorem 1 needs a closed finite-dimensional subspace, which fails when $\mathcal{V}$ is infinite-dimensional. Here is a proof that verifies the answer directly.

:::theorem[Representer theorem for operator-valued kernels]
Let $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_N \in \mathcal{V}$ solve

$$
\sum_{j=1}^N \mathcal{K}(u_i, u_j)\,\alpha_j + \lambda\,\alpha_i = v_i, \qquad i = 1, \dots, N .
$$

Then $\hat f = \sum_j \mathcal{K}(\cdot, u_j)\,\alpha_j$ is the unique minimiser.
:::

:::proof
**Step 0. A solution exists.** The block operator $\mathbb{K}$ on $\mathcal{V}^N$ is positive semidefinite (Definition 4), so $\mathbb{K} + \lambda\mathcal{I}$ satisfies $\langle\alpha, (\mathbb{K} + \lambda\mathcal{I})\alpha\rangle \ge \lambda\lVert\alpha\rVert^2$ and is invertible.

**Step 1. Perturb.** For any $h \in \mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}$, write $r_i = v_i - \hat f(u_i)$ and expand $J(\hat f + h)$:

$$
J(\hat f + h) = \sum_i\lVert r_i - h(u_i)\rVert^2 + \lambda\lVert\hat f + h\rVert^2 .
$$

**Step 2. Expand both squares.**

$$
J(\hat f + h) - J(\hat f) = \underbrace{-2\sum_i\langle r_i, h(u_i)\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} + 2\lambda\langle\hat f, h\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}}}_{\text{linear in } h} + \sum_i\lVert h(u_i)\rVert^2 + \lambda\lVert h\rVert^2 .
$$

**Step 3. Use the linear system.** It says exactly $r_i = v_i - \sum_j\mathcal{K}(u_i, u_j)\alpha_j = \lambda\alpha_i$.

**Step 4. Use the reproducing property** (Lemma 3 with $c = \alpha_i$): $\langle\alpha_i, h(u_i)\rangle_{\mathcal{V}} = \langle\mathcal{K}(\cdot, u_i)\alpha_i, h\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}}$. Summing,

$$
\sum_i\langle r_i, h(u_i)\rangle = \lambda\sum_i\langle\mathcal{K}(\cdot, u_i)\alpha_i, h\rangle = \lambda\langle\hat f, h\rangle .
$$

**Step 5. The linear terms cancel.** By Step 4, the bracket in Step 2 is $-2\lambda\langle\hat f, h\rangle + 2\lambda\langle\hat f, h\rangle = 0$.

**Step 6. Conclude.** $J(\hat f + h) - J(\hat f) = \sum_i\lVert h(u_i)\rVert^2 + \lambda\lVert h\rVert^2 \ge 0$, with equality only for $h = 0$.
:::

For a separable kernel on a grid of $m$ output points, $\mathcal{T}$ becomes an $m\times m$ matrix $\mathbf{T}$ and the system is $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{T} + \lambda\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{V}$, solved by Proposition 2 with $p = m$. (With uniform quadrature weights the grid inner product is $\boldsymbol{a}^\top\boldsymbol{b}/m$; the constant is absorbed into $\mathbf{T}$.)

## 5. The Gaussian-process view

A $\mathcal{V}$-valued GP $f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, \mathcal{K})$ is a random map from $\mathcal{U}$ to $\mathcal{V}$ whose values at any finite set of inputs are jointly Gaussian, with $\mathbb{E}\big[\langle f(u), a\rangle\langle f(u'), b\rangle\big] = \langle a, \mathcal{K}(u, u')\,b\rangle$. Conditioning works exactly as in GP Section 6, block by block. For separable kernels, one choice of noise makes the result strikingly simple.

:::proposition[Separable GP operator with matched noise]
Let $\mathcal{K}(u, u') = k(u, u')\,\mathbf{T}$ on a grid, with $\mathbf{T}$ positive definite, and observe $\boldsymbol{v}_i = \boldsymbol{f}(u_i) + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i$ with independent $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \lambda\mathbf{T})$. With $\boldsymbol{w}(u) = (\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{k}_u$ and $\boldsymbol{k}_u = [k(u_1, u), \dots, k(u_N, u)]^\top$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{f}(u) \mid \text{data}] &= \sum_{i=1}^N w_i(u)\,\boldsymbol{v}_i, \\
\operatorname{Cov}[\boldsymbol{f}(u) \mid \text{data}] &= \big(k(u, u) - \boldsymbol{k}_u^\top(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{k}_u\big)\,\mathbf{T}.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Stack the observations** input by input, $\boldsymbol{v} = [\boldsymbol{v}_1; \dots; \boldsymbol{v}_N]$. Signal and noise are independent, so by GP Lemma 3 their covariances add:

$$
\operatorname{Cov}[\boldsymbol{v}] = \mathbf{K} \otimes \mathbf{T} + \mathbf{I} \otimes (\lambda\mathbf{T}) = (\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I}) \otimes \mathbf{T}.
$$

(The last step: block $(i, j)$ of both sides is $(K_{ij} + \lambda\delta_{ij})\mathbf{T}$.)

**Step 2. The cross-covariance** between $\boldsymbol{f}(u)$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$ has blocks $k(u, u_i)\mathbf{T}$, that is, $\boldsymbol{k}_u^\top \otimes \mathbf{T}$.

**Step 3. Invert with Lemma 2.** $\big((\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I}) \otimes \mathbf{T}\big)^{-1} = (\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{T}^{-1}$.

**Step 4. The mean** (GP Lemma 5), using the mixed product twice:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\boldsymbol{k}_u^\top \otimes \mathbf{T})\big((\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{T}^{-1}\big)\boldsymbol{v}
&= \big(\boldsymbol{k}_u^\top(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{T}\mathbf{T}^{-1}\big)\boldsymbol{v} \\
&= (\boldsymbol{w}(u)^\top \otimes \mathbf{I})\,\boldsymbol{v} = \sum_i w_i(u)\,\boldsymbol{v}_i .
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5. The covariance** (GP Lemma 5), by the same two steps:

$$
k(u, u)\mathbf{T} - \big(\boldsymbol{k}_u^\top(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{k}_u\big) \otimes \big(\mathbf{T}\mathbf{T}^{-1}\mathbf{T}\big) = \big(k(u, u) - \boldsymbol{k}_u^\top(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\boldsymbol{k}_u\big)\,\mathbf{T}.
$$
:::

Two readings. First, $\mathbf{T}$ has cancelled from the mean: **the prediction is a kernel-weighted average of the training output functions**, with weights set entirely by how similar $u$ is to each training input. Second, the uncertainty is a scalar, the ordinary GP variance in input space, times a fixed output shape $\mathbf{T}$. The opening figure is this proposition: the band's width is that scalar.

:::remark[With a linear kernel, uncertainty is the part of the input you have never seen]
Take $k(u, u') = \langle u, u'\rangle_{L^2}$ and let $\lambda \to 0$.

**Step 1.** $\mathbf{K}$ is the Gram matrix of the training inputs, $K_{ij} = \langle u_i, u_j\rangle$, and $\boldsymbol{k}_u$ has entries $\langle u_i, u\rangle$.

**Step 2.** The orthogonal projection of $u$ onto $\operatorname{span}\{u_i\}$ is $\Pi u = \sum_i c_iu_i$ with $\boldsymbol{c} = \mathbf{K}^{-1}\boldsymbol{k}_u$ (the normal equations), and $\lVert\Pi u\rVert^2 = \boldsymbol{c}^\top\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{c} = \boldsymbol{k}_u^\top\mathbf{K}^{-1}\boldsymbol{k}_u$.

**Step 3.** By Pythagoras, the variance factor is

$$
k(u, u) - \boldsymbol{k}_u^\top\mathbf{K}^{-1}\boldsymbol{k}_u = \lVert u\rVert^2 - \lVert\Pi u\rVert^2 = \lVert u - \Pi u\rVert^2 .
$$

The posterior variance is the energy of the input outside everything the training set has shown. In the demo, **Add a wiggle** adds $0.35\sin(2\pi\cdot 11z)$, a frequency absent from every training input, and the band grows accordingly. (In the code of Section 9 the same experiment returns exactly $\lVert 0.3\sin\rVert^2 = 0.045$.)
:::

### A ladder of simplifications

Exact inference with a general operator-valued kernel is hopeless at realistic sizes. Every practical method buys speed with an assumption. The ladder below collects the ones in this post; each rung keeps the previous assumptions.

:::remark[POD-GP: the low-rank rung, as computational mechanics uses it]
The most widely used operator GP in computational mechanics is two familiar steps glued together (Guo and Hesthaven, CMAME 2018).

**Step 1. Compress the outputs with POD.** Stack the training outputs on the grid as the rows of $\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ (subtract the mean first). The leading $R$ right singular vectors $\boldsymbol{\phi}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{\phi}_R$ of $\mathbf{V}$, the proper orthogonal decomposition modes, are the best rank-$R$ basis for the outputs in the least-squares sense. Each output becomes $R$ coefficients, $a_{ir} = \boldsymbol{\phi}_r^\top\boldsymbol{v}_i$.

**Step 2. Regress each coefficient with its own scalar GP.** $a_r(u) \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_r)$, independent across $r$, and predict $\boldsymbol{f}(u) = \sum_r a_r(u)\,\boldsymbol{\phi}_r$.

**Step 3. Read off the operator-valued kernel.** By independence, only the $r = s$ terms survive in the covariance:

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\big[\boldsymbol{f}(u), \boldsymbol{f}(u')\big] = \sum_{r,s}\operatorname{Cov}\big[a_r(u), a_s(u')\big]\,\boldsymbol{\phi}_r\boldsymbol{\phi}_s^\top = \sum_{r=1}^R k_r(u, u')\,\boldsymbol{\phi}_r\boldsymbol{\phi}_r^\top .
$$

That is a linear model of coregionalisation (Example 1) with rank-one output matrices $\mathbf{B}_r = \boldsymbol{\phi}_r\boldsymbol{\phi}_r^\top$ taken from the data. With a single shared $k$ it is the separable kernel $k(u, u')\,\mathbf{T}$ with $\mathbf{T} = \sum_r\boldsymbol{\phi}_r\boldsymbol{\phi}_r^\top$ of rank $R$: the fourth rung of the ladder.

**Step 4. The cost.** $R$ independent $N\times N$ GPs plus one SVD: $O(RN^3 + \min(N, m)\,Nm)$, independent of the mesh after the SVD. The price is the same as DeepONet's: predictions cannot leave the span of the $R$ modes, so features the training snapshots never contained are invisible to both the mean and the uncertainty.
:::

## 6. Kernels on function inputs

The input kernel $k(u, u')$ compares two *functions*, observed on grids $\{z_j\}_{j=1}^m$ as vectors $\boldsymbol{u}$. The obvious choice, an RBF on the Euclidean distance of the vectors, has a hidden defect:

$$
\lVert\boldsymbol{u} - \boldsymbol{u}'\rVert_2^2 = \sum_{j=1}^m\big(u(z_j) - u'(z_j)\big)^2 \approx m\int_\Omega\big(u - u'\big)^2\,dz .
$$

It grows linearly with the resolution, so refining the grid silently changes the kernel. Use quadrature instead, $\lVert u - u'\rVert_{L^2}^2 \approx \sum_j \omega_j\big(u(z_j) - u'(z_j)\big)^2$ with weights $\omega_j$ ($1/m$ on a uniform grid), which converges as $m \to \infty$. Then the same kernel, and the same trained model, can be evaluated on inputs sampled on any sufficiently fine grid. This is what *discretisation invariance* means for kernels.

The choice of kernel on inputs is an assumption about the operator:

- **Linear**, $k(u, u') = \langle u, u'\rangle_{L^2}$. By Proposition 6 the mean is linear in $u$ (the weights $\boldsymbol{w}(u)$ are), so the model can only represent linear operators, and it extrapolates them perfectly. Heat diffusion is linear; this is why **Double it** works.
- **RBF on $L^2$**, $k(u, u') = \exp\!\big(-\lVert u - u'\rVert_{L^2}^2/2\ell^2\big)$. Nonlinear and local: far from all training inputs, $\boldsymbol{k}_u \to \mathbf{0}$, the mean returns to zero and the variance to the prior. Safe, but it cannot extrapolate.
- **Sobolev distances**, adding $\lVert\nabla u - \nabla u'\rVert^2$, make two inputs similar only when their shapes, not just their values, agree.

## 7. Bridges to neural operators

- **DeepONet** predicts $\mathcal{G}(u)(z) \approx \sum_{r=1}^R b_r(u)\,t_r(z)$: a branch network of the input times trunk functions of the output location. A separable kernel with a rank-$R$ output operator $\mathcal{T} = \sum_r t_r\langle t_r, \cdot\rangle$ has the same structure, because every prediction $\sum_i k(u, u_i)\,\mathcal{T}\alpha_i$ lies in the range of $\mathcal{T}$, which is $\operatorname{span}\{t_r\}$. DeepONet learns the basis by gradient descent; the kernel model fixes it and solves for the rest in closed form.
- **Fourier neural operators** build each layer from a convolution, which is multiplication in the Fourier basis. Translation-equivariant operators are exactly the ones that are diagonal in that basis, the heat operator of Section 9 being the cleanest example. A stationary output covariance $\mathcal{T}$ is diagonal there too, which is why spectral methods suit both.
- **POD-GP** (Guo and Hesthaven, 2018) replaces DeepONet's learned trunk by POD modes of the training outputs and regresses the coefficients with scalar GPs: the same low-rank structure, solved in closed form (Remark after the ladder).
- **Linearised neural operators are curried GPs.** Magnani et al. (ICML 2025) linearise a trained neural operator under a Gaussian weight belief and curry the resulting scalar GP into a function-valued one (Remark after Proposition 4).
- **Infinitely wide neural operators are GPs on functions.** de Souza, Zhu, Cunningham, Saporito, Mesquita and Deisenroth (NeurIPS 2025) show when randomly initialised neural operators converge, as their width grows, to function-valued GPs, and compute the resulting covariance functions for the Fourier neural operator. The kernel view and the network view of operator learning are two limits of one model.

In my own work with Rajdip Nayek and Souvik Chakraborty, the kernel and the network meet in the other direction: a neural operator supplies the kernel of a GP ([CMAME 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15618); [CMAME 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.10972)), and local kernel interactions are assembled into a scalable global operator ([J. Comput. Phys. 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15906), with Tapas Tripura).

## 8. Theory you should know exists

- **Rates.** For vector-valued kernel ridge regression with outputs in a Hilbert space, Caponnetto and De Vito (2007) prove minimax-optimal learning rates under smoothness ("source") and capacity assumptions, and their setting assumes $\mathcal{K}(u, u)$ is trace class, the condition of Proposition 5.
- **Universality.** Whether $\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{K}}$ can approximate every continuous operator is characterised by Carmeli, De Vito, Toigo and Umanità (2010).
- **Functional responses.** Kadri, Duflos, Preux, Canu, Rakotomamonjy and Audiffren (2016) develop operator-valued kernels for function-valued outputs, with algorithms and experiments on speech and audio.

## 9. A worked example you can run: the heat operator

The heat equation on the periodic interval, $\partial_t v = \partial_z^2 v$ with $v(\cdot, 0) = u$, defines the solution operator $\mathcal{G}_t : u \mapsto v(\cdot, t)$, written $e^{t\Delta}$.

:::proposition[The heat operator is diagonal in the Fourier basis]
If $u(z) = \sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\hat u_k\,e^{2\pi ikz}$, then $(e^{t\Delta}u)(z) = \sum_k e^{-4\pi^2k^2t}\,\hat u_k\,e^{2\pi ikz}$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Fourier modes are eigenfunctions of $\partial_z^2$.** Differentiating twice, $\partial_z^2\,e^{2\pi ikz} = (2\pi ik)^2e^{2\pi ikz} = -4\pi^2k^2\,e^{2\pi ikz}$.

**Step 2. Expand the solution in the same basis.** Write $v(z, t) = \sum_k c_k(t)\,e^{2\pi ikz}$ with $c_k(0) = \hat u_k$.

**Step 3. Substitute into the equation.** By Step 1, $\sum_k c_k'(t)\,e^{2\pi ikz} = \sum_k -4\pi^2k^2c_k(t)\,e^{2\pi ikz}$. The modes are orthogonal, so the coefficients match one by one: $c_k' = -4\pi^2k^2c_k$.

**Step 4. Solve each scalar ODE.** $c_k(t) = e^{-4\pi^2k^2t}\,\hat u_k$.
:::

Each mode decays at its own rate, and high frequencies die fastest: the heat operator is a low-pass filter, and $-4\pi^2k^2$ are the eigenvalues of the Laplacian ([the Laplacian post](/aboutme/blog/one-operator-i-keep-coming-back-to/) tells the longer story).

<video src="/aboutme/blog/operator/heat-modes.mp4" autoplay muted loop playsinline controls poster="/aboutme/blog/operator/heat-modes.jpg"></video>

The code below learns $e^{t\Delta}$ from 200 examples with the linear kernel and Proposition 6.

```python
import numpy as np

m, N, t, lam = 128, 200, 0.002, 1e-6
k = np.fft.rfftfreq(m, 1 / m)                        # wavenumbers 0, 1, ..., m/2
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def random_inputs(n, width=6.0):
    c = rng.standard_normal((n, k.size)) + 1j * rng.standard_normal((n, k.size))
    return np.fft.irfft(c * np.exp(-0.5 * (k / width) ** 2), m)   # smooth periodic functions

def heat(U):                                         # exact solution operator, one row per function
    return np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(U) * np.exp(-4 * np.pi**2 * k**2 * t), m)

def k_lin(A, B):                                     # <u, u'> in L^2, by quadrature on the grid
    return A @ B.T / m

U = random_inputs(N); V = heat(U)                    # training pairs
Us = random_inputs(5)                                # test inputs
Wt = np.linalg.solve(k_lin(U, U) + lam * np.eye(N), k_lin(U, Us))   # N x 5 weights w(u)
mean = Wt.T @ V                                      # Proposition 6: weighted sum of training outputs
var = np.diag(k_lin(Us, Us)) - np.sum(k_lin(U, Us) * Wt, 0)          # multiplies T at every z
err = np.linalg.norm(mean - heat(Us)) / np.linalg.norm(heat(Us))
print(f"relative error {err:.2e}; variance factors {np.round(var, 6)}")
# relative error 8.02e-05; variance factors [0. 0. 0. 0. 0.]

z = np.arange(m) / m
odd = Us + 0.3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 40 * z)          # add a frequency no training input contains
Wo = np.linalg.solve(k_lin(U, U) + lam * np.eye(N), k_lin(U, odd))
print(np.diag(k_lin(odd, odd)) - np.sum(k_lin(U, odd) * Wo, 0))     # [0.045 ...] = ||0.3 sin||^2
```

## Questions

:::question
Why is $k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}')\mathbf{B}$ with an indefinite $\mathbf{B}$ not a valid kernel, even when $k$ is?
:::

:::answer
Take a single input, $N = 1$. The block Gram matrix is $k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x})\mathbf{B}$, and if $\mathbf{B}$ has a negative eigenvalue with eigenvector $\boldsymbol{c}$, then $\boldsymbol{c}^\top k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x})\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{c} < 0$ whenever $k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}) > 0$.
:::

:::question
With $N = 500$ training pairs on a grid of $m = 2000$ points, how many unknowns does the direct solve have, and what does the Kronecker trick factor instead?
:::

:::answer
$Nm = 10^6$ unknowns, a $10^6\times 10^6$ system. The Kronecker trick eigendecomposes a $500\times 500$ and a $2000\times 2000$ matrix.
:::

:::question
In Proposition 6, the output covariance $\mathbf{T}$ disappears from the posterior mean. What, then, is it for?
:::

:::answer
It shapes the uncertainty (the posterior covariance is a scalar times $\mathbf{T}$), and so it determines what posterior samples look like and how errors at different output locations are correlated. With a different noise model (for example $\lambda\mathbf{I}$ instead of $\lambda\mathbf{T}$) it also enters the mean.
:::

:::question
Why can't a GP operator with output covariance $\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{I}$ be refined to arbitrarily fine grids?
:::

:::answer
$\operatorname{tr}\mathcal{I} = \infty$, so by Proposition 5 its samples have infinite expected energy. On an $m$-point grid the trace is $m$, so sample norms grow with resolution instead of converging.
:::
